utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are a few matters we have to deal with, but I'd first like to give an opportunity to Mr. Jordash to raise a matter he wishes to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. Unfortunately, we return to the issue of the accused's health and a request to Your Honours to intervene at this stage to order the Registry to serve immediately the accused's medical records relating to his psychiatric treatment to date, since being incarcerated in the UNDU. On the 28th of October, 2011, the Defence requested the medical files from OLAD since it hadn't received any medical records since the 20th of September, 2010. Your Honours will recall that we made a first request for medical records in early 2010. The Defence made a further request on the 28th of November, 2011, since the first submission of those notes was incomplete. The next day, OLAD provided further medical files. On the 24th of January, 2012, the Defence orally applied to the Trial Chamber seeking assistance to have certain questions relating to Mr. Stanisic's treatment answered, in large part because we could not obtain or had not obtained an answer on the requests for records from OLAD. On the 26th of January, 2012, the Trial Chamber ordered the reporting medical officer to answer certain questions, particularly in regards to the psychiatric services provided to Mr. Stanisic. On the 30th of January, 2012, the RMO responded to the questions, noting inter alia that Mr. Stanisic receives medication and psychotherapeutic services from Dr. Petrovic every four to six weeks. On the basis of these answers, and on the same day, the Defence wrote to OLAD requesting disclosure of any and all records relating to Mr. Stanisic's treatment by Dr. Petrovic. And I note at this point, by 30th January, 2012, that request had, in effect, been outstanding for the best part of 18 months. On the 2nd of February, 2012, OLAD responded, and agreed to provide these records specifically. In lieu of the immediate service of those records, OLAD provided a summary compiled by Dr. Petrovic which indicated, amongst other aspects, that her view was that Mr. Stanisic's treatment, in particular his psychotherapy, was insufficient. She also indicated, contrary to what had been reported to the reporting medical officer, that she met with Mr. Stanisic every seven weeks and not every four to six weeks. There have been several attempts by the Stanisic Defence, authorised by Mr. Stanisic and instructed by Mr. Stanisic, to obtain Dr. Petrovic's records. In sum, the Defence has not received those records. And despite numerous requests and despite indicating our deep concern about Dr. Petrovic's stated view, that Mr. Stanisic's treatment, his psychotherapy, was insufficient, we still await those records. In the absence of those records, we, the authorised representatives of Mr. Stanisic, must advance on the basis of what we know. And what we know from Ms. Petrovic is that it is her view that Mr. Stanisic's treatment within the UNDU is insufficient, in relation to his serious psychiatric condition. Your Honours will appreciate that failure to provide sufficient medical services is in direct contravention of the UN General Assembly Resolution 44/111; it is in direct violation of numerous international instruments, from Article 25(1) of The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the ICCPR, and the Human Rights Committee and its various declarations. As I have indicated, we must proceed, in the absence of notes which we have persistently and consistently requested, on the basis of what we know, which is Dr. Petrovic's view. And that is why we now seek, as the last resort, Your Honours' intervention at this stage. We also note that in the past, when requesting medical notes and querying whether other medical notes have existed, the Registry have responded rapidly or relatively rapidly. It is with this issue, where the prima facie evidence indicates that Mr. Stanisic's treatment is insufficient, where the Registry have, if I may use colloquialism, dragged their heels, to say the least. And we ask for Your Honours' intervention at this stage because it is the least severe remedy. Other remedies which we are at the door of requesting is a hearing on the fitness of the accused, fitness to participate and fitness to be detained; two, an immediate suspension of the trial proceedings pending a proper assessment of Mr. Stanisic's treatment within the UNDU; three, an immediate release within Holland or in Belgrade to allow him to obtain adequate medical treatment himself; and finally, a review of the Registry's refusal to provide reasonable information to the accused. And that application will involve an application to investigate whether the Registry are seeking deliberately to conceal bad medical care in the UNDU. And so we request at this stage that Your Honours order the disclosure of those notes forth with. It relates to this trial and its ability to continue in light of Mr. Stanisic's fitness, and I do use the word fitness. It's not an all or nothing affair. Is he fit to participate in the Strugar sense is one question. Is his health deteriorating as a result of the proceedings is another question which, I submit, engages Your Honours. Is he fit to be detained in lieu of the medical treatment being offered is another question which engages Your Honours. Those are questions which we will be forced to pursue. But we are not there. Where we are is a request to Your Honours to order disclosure of the medical notes forth with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those are your submissions. May I take it that the other parties have no specific interest in making submissions on the matter. Mr. Jordash, I took it from your words that you are aware, of course - that's not new for you - that, of course, the Chamber always has to keep in mind what is treatment and medical care and what's the impact on the proceedings, and I think you have addressed us also to explain what, in this case, at this moment, the link would be. That's one. Second, the matter has the attention of the Chamber. It did not arise for the first time in these -- since this -- the beginning of this year. Please be convinced that the matter has the attention of the Chamber, and it's -- now your request is clearly on the record. We'll consider it. The third -- but that's just a very simple question. You have focussed on what you say is the opinion of Dr. Petrovic as to the inadequacy or insufficiency of the psychiatric treatment. Now, may I take it that Mr. Stanisic was more or less aware about the frequency with which he saw Dr. Petrovic. Has there any -- ever been a request for a -- for a more intense psychiatric treatment or has it ever been advised, to your knowledge? To say, Well, I see a psychiatrist once every six or seven weeks, that's insufficient; could I see a psychiatrist every week or every second week or ... Has ever such a request -- because that's the part of the treatment with which everything starts, I would say. The -- if you think that you get insufficient or inadequate treatment, you seek better treatment or more adequate treatment. Has there ever been a request to intensify the contacts with someone who could provide psychiatric care?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The simple answer is, I don't know the answer to that question. I do know this: That I've spoken to Mr. Stanisic on a number of occasions and he would like to see Dr. Petrovic more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He's explained that frustration to me on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whether or not that could be Dr. Petrovic or not is another matter. But perhaps that -- that answer to that question, whether it -- that has ever been expressed, a more intensified or more frequent consultation with a psychiatrist or psychologist, whether that has ever been requested, because that would, my view, not ignoring all the matters you're raising, would be the first step if there's any reason to believe that the psychiatric or psychological consultations are insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I would put it slightly differently to what Your Honour has said. I would say that the first step is for the professionals to indicate to Mr. Stanisic whether he has sufficient treatment. And I -- my experience is that a patient is the worst person to indicate or to assess their own treatment, often. Especially, if I may say so, men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's leave this part of the debate where it is. I -- there may be a role for all. Let's -- it is -- your request is clearly on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no further questions. If you'd like to add, have you an opportunity to do so. But please be convinced that the matter has our full attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've just been passed a note from Mr. Stanisic who notes: On a number of occasions I have sought to see Petrovic and the Court doctor but with no success. So that may answer Your Honours' question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not entirely. Because the answer is not a direct answer to the question. But at least, communication seems to be far from perfect, to say the least. Yes. Then, in relation to the next witness to be called, I would like to briefly go into private session. No, perhaps I first deal with a matter for which we do not have to go into private session. The Chamber has received the Simatovic urgent Defence request for an adjournment which was filed on the 20th of February of this year. The Chamber wonders whether an expedited response could be received. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. We could provide our response on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not any earlier? Because in view of the urgency of the request and the preparations the Simatovic Defence will have to make for their next witnesses, is there any way you could respond earlier?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Then we'll do so on Friday. Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about Thursday end of business, would that do?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As you -- as you wish, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I put a question to you, whether that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will do so, end of day Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: End of the day on Thursday. Mr. Petrovic, just for your information: Until a decision has been taken on your motion, you should prepare for calling your witnesses as they were scheduled. So you cannot anticipate, hoping or expecting, that the motion would be granted and then to have no witnesses here. You may have noticed that we encouraged the Prosecution to respond very quickly, and the Chamber will also try to deliver its decision as soon as possible; but meanwhile, the trial proceeds as scheduled. And you should take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you switch on your microphone, that would assist, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We will do our utmost, but, with your leave, I will try to -- or we will try to do as you say tomorrow. But give me time until tomorrow, please, to let you know what that will be exactly, whether we will be able to call the first witnesses as listed before or we will have to change something in the order of witnesses. So please give me time until tomorrow. It is quite possible, in view of what you just said, that we will be forced to change the order of witnesses somewhat, in light of the situation as described in our motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please consult with the Prosecution before you change the order of calling of witnesses, and seek an approach which will not meet objections by the Prosecution. I do understand your request to be that you would like to have until tomorrow not to find out on whether you can present witnesses but in which order you'd like to present them, if that -- if that deviates from the order as scheduled until now. Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit, the submission we made yesterday is not manipulative in any way. We are not trying to achieve anything. It just reflects the current situation on our Defence. We can seek to apportion blame in various ways, but it's not for me to speak about that now. Quite simply, what was stated yesterday is exactly the situation. Now, in light of what you just said, can I try to see with the lead counsel whether there is another way out, another possibility to meet your instructions and requirements. However, at this moment I'm not in a position to say any more than what was stated in our submission yesterday. I kindly ask for your understanding. Mr. Bakrac is currently with the witness who is supposed to appear tomorrow. I can only repeat my request for time until tomorrow for us to be able to state our position and our possibilities at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could I just seek clarification from Mr. Petrovic that -- that DSF-015 and -16 would most definitely not start next week. In other words, if -- if, whatever the Chamber may decide with regard to the adjournment, other witnesses would be put on the list, and then you would inform us, if I understand correctly, of those witnesses by tomorrow. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure my learned friend understood me correctly. I cannot offer now any further information above what our yesterday's submission stated. And with the Court's leave we will inform you further about our possibilities and our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The message of the Chamber was quite clear: That, awaiting a decision on your request, no Court time should be lost by non-availability of witnesses. That's the clear message I think I gave. And that's not for you to consider but that is for you to observe. Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you will now be examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness. Would you kindly state your name for the record, your date of birth, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Risto Seovac, born on 5 April 1955 in the village of Mrko [phoen], Han Pijesak municipality, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel must turn off his microphone while the witness is answering. Audibility is considerably reduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you are invited to switch off your microphone when the witness is answering the questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us about your educational attainment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I finished primary school in a place called Pjelovac [phoen], Han Pijesak municipality. Then the secondary school for internal affairs in Sremska Kamenica, Serbia. And the higher administration school attached to the law school of the university in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was your first job, and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first job was a trainee policeman. And on the 1st July --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I became a policeman in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you transferred from Titova Uzice at some point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The year is missing from the transcript. The interpreter could not catch the year. The 1st of July of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1974.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were transferred to a different job in a different town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I took the state examination while I was still a trainee in 1974 I was transferred to the SUP in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were your duties in the SUP of Bajina Basta, and until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the time I took the state examination in January 1975, I was a policeman until 1977, and from 1977 on, I was the sector leader in the traffic police department until I finished my studies. And then I continued as sector leader until 1981, when I became deputy police commander in the Bajina Basta SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Until what year were you deputy commander of the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1st October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What year were you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 31st December, 1987. Sorry, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you tell us in one sentence where Bajina Basta is located geographically. What is on the opposite side of Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bajina Basta is a municipality that belongs to the Zlatibor district. It rounds off the central part of the Drina valley. Opposite is Bosnia and Herzegovina. And on the other side is the territory of Skelani, nowadays Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is between Bajina Basta and the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when a check-point was placed on the bridge connecting the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A check-point was set up on the junction of roads, one of which goes to Skelani and the other one along the Drina towards Perucac, sometime in October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when this check-point was reorganised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, pursuant to a decision of the higher authorities, it was turned into a border crossing, and it was moved further to be next to the bridge. And it became officially a border crossing on the 7th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you, witness, get any assignments regarding this border crossing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. By virtue of a decision of the MUP of Serbia, I was appointed commander of the check-point station of Bajina Basta on the border crossing, and I was placed to work on the border crossing itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The record says -- could you repeat to us the exact name of that station that you led. What is the full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Police station for the inspection of border crossing, Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To whom was this police station and its commander, to whom were they answerable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are answerable to the MUP of Serbia, that is, the administration supervising border crossings, of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where is that administration located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The base of the MUP of Serbia, in Belgrade, at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To what department within the MUP of Serbia does your station belong, as well as the entire administration overseeing border crossings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They both belong to the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In this time since 1992 that you have headed this station, can you describe to us how the crossings of armed people or uniformed people from Bosnia and Herzegovina into the Republic of Serbia has been regulated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By decree of the government, that is to say, the Federal Executive Council, number 2, dated 1st May, 1992, border crossings towards Bosnia and Herzegovina were designated, as well as border crossings controlled by the United Nations as they were known at the time. Meaning Krajina, Slovenia. The same enactment stipulates how the border crossing may be change -- crossed, that is to say, only with a valid passport, or a valid ID in the case of neighbouring territories. The same enactment stipulates that the border may not be crossed carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If somebody from Bosnia turned up at your border crossing carrying weapons, what was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would not be allowed to enter the territory of Serbia. They would be turned back into the territory of the neighbouring country from which they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If somebody from Serbia tried to leave Serbia across the border that you controlled carrying weapons, what would be your reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such people would be intercepted and turned over to the local police who would process them further, maybe charge them with possession of weapons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Specifically on your border crossing have there ever been any situations like that: Attempts by people from the other side of the Drina to enter Serbia carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have to bear in mind that almost 50 per cent of the urban population in Bajina Basta are Serbs from the territory of Srebrenica, that is to say, Republika Srpska. Problems were numerous. People were constantly trying to come back home carrying the weapons they had on the front line, so we had to deal with this problem more or less constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say you turned these people back. You turned them back to whom? Where would they go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the border crossing, the neighbouring party controls the border crossing. And if that person does not meet the requirements to enter our country, we turned that person back to the authorities of the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to you, which other policemen, which other officials, oversaw this border crossing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were also members of the military police of the 16th Battalion of -- 16th Border Battalion of the Army of Yugoslavia, and the customs service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why the military police was present? Whom did they have jurisdiction over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had jurisdiction over uniformed persons carrying weapons. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any jurisdiction over the military policemen manning the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have any direct command or control over them. They were working alongside us, doing their part of the job. We checked that people had proper documents to enter our territory, and they did other work that was not in our hands or responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honour, it is time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a suitable moment for the break. And we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start. At the same time, you give us quite a bit of homework now and then for the breaks. Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to continue? And before we do so, one observation. Mr. Jordash, I do not know whether the Stanisic Defence had any intention to respond to the urgent motion filed yesterday by the Simatovic Defence. If so, I'd like to set the deadline for you to Thursday as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, at the time when you were the commander of the police station for state border control, what was the territory controlled by your police station? What was under your authority at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the regulations and in keeping with the document on the establishment of the police station, was in charge of the road leading between one state to the next and 50 metres on each of the sides of the road [as interpreted]. That's the area concerned border crossing. And in depth, the length was 100 metres, not further than that. Beyond those parameters, those police stations that controlled border crossings did not have any authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have noticed that I am waiting for you to finish your answer, because everything is interpreted. Who controls the area beyond the area that was under the control of the police station for border crossing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the army, or, rather, its border units. In our case, that was the 16th Border-Crossing Detachment that was deployed in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us who controlled the Perucac dam that was several kilometres up the stream from Bajina Basta? Who controlled the crossing across that facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bajina Basta, i.e., the dam, was not a regular border crossing. And it was under the control of the same entity that controlled the border, which was the Army of Yugoslavia. The Army of Yugoslavia controlled all the facilities in the immediate vicinity of the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could vehicles also cross the border across the Perucac dam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if in the vicinity of the dam there was a Yugoslav army facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a watch tower of the Yugoslav army that controlled the border crossing from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when the territory of Skelani came under attack? And if it did, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the 16th of January, 1993, in the early morning hours. As far as I can remember, that was around 5.00 in the morning. An attack was launched from the depth of the territory from the direction of Srebrenica, towards a Skelanica [phoen] settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, what happened with the population of Skelani and the surrounding villages at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All those who were fleeing before the attack, all those who survived and could move about, came to the bridge. That was their only way to get across the river to the other side and save themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, where is the border on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that you cannot navigate across the Drina, and according to the international regulations, if a border goes along a non-navigable river, then the border would be in its middle, which means that two-thirds of the bridge were under the authority of the Republic of Serbia and one third was under the authority of Bosnia and Herzegovina, i.e., the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned that the population started fleeing across the bridge towards Serbia. Was fire opened on the inhabitants of Skelani and other villages who were on the way to Serbia on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the population and on our facilities and our staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Where did fire come from? And what area came under that fire on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The entire area of Skelani was under fire. And since the population was coming to the bridge in a funnel-shaped manner, the fire followed them and came closer to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in this part of the bridge that is in the territory of the Republic of Serbia, and in the area around your police station, were there any casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were about 40 dead and about 60 injured in that area from the middle of the bridge up to our facilities, on that part of the embankment and the river shore.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that day was fire opened on Bajina Basta as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time when fire was opened on Skelani, fire was also opened on the road leading from Skelani to Bajina Basta. Some five or six mortar shells fell on the -- on the road on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what happened to the population of Bajina Basta on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since fire was opened on the city, on the city centre, and on the hotel - you can still see the damage on the hotel - the population started withdrawing towards the depth of the territory, i.e., towards Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on that day -- or, rather, first tell me, as far as you know, What was the total number of casualties among the civilian population of Skelani and surrounding villages on that day as a result of the attack that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but approximately there were about 60 dead in total and approximately about a hundred injured, severely and slightly injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, among those who were killed in the territory of the Republic of Serbia on the bridge and around your police station, who were they? Were they militarily able-bodied men, civilians? Who were the casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The casualties were both members of the Army of Republika Srpska from Skelani as well as women and children. I believe that on that day four our five children were killed. The youngest was four.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when the Army of Yugoslavia got involved in the defence of Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After fire was opened on the road and the city centre, the Army of Yugoslavia, i.e., 16th Border-Crossing Battalion, got involved in order to stop the attack and in order to allow the population to withdraw from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did some MUP units come to their aid as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime around midday PJPs came to aid the Army of Yugoslavia. They were from Uzice, from Uzice MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the record we can see "PJPs from Uzice." Yes. Yes, that's good. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, after this event, did some MUP officials also arrive in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the following day, sometime in the afternoon, the prime minister, Mr. Sainovic, came to Bajina Basta and to my border crossing, to my police station. I apologise, that was later. It was actually the chief of the public security sector - Mr. Badza - arrived with other service members.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who came with Badza? Did you know any of those people who came with Badza to Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The chief of the department, the then-commander of the PJPs, Obrad Stevanovic. I believe that the chief of the state security department was also there, but I'm not sure about that. And some local officials. The local leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know why Radovan Stojicic came to Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After all those developments and events and after our reports, he came to establish what had happened and to take measures in order to protect one part of the state territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, What measures did Stojicic put in place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that same day, a staff was established, a staff of PJPs, in Bajina Basta. And I believe that Obrad Stevanovic was appointed its commander. From then on he was supposed to devise further measures and put them in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where the staff was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was located in -- on the premises of the Secretariat of the Interior in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you have any communication with the staff at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only when I received instructions from my administration, if I needed to go there to request something, or something like that. All the contacts that they had were with my administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you contacted somebody in the staff? And if you did, who was it and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were a police station under establishment. We did not have any equipment. My administration recommended that I should contact the staff commander and request the radio sets that I didn't have and that I needed to ask them to give me as much as they could. Those were my contacts with them around that time. And not only radio sets, but also other equipment as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us - you say that you contacted the staff commander - who was that? Who did you talk to about the equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon the recommendation of my superior command, I talked directly to the staff commander, Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned just a minute ago the Uzice detachment of PJPs. Did there come a time when some other members and some other PJP detachments came from other cities in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the staff was established and when the staff took over its task, additional forces were deployed from all over Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, just one sentence, please, to explain to us: Who were members of PJPs at the time? How were they recruited? Which policemen constituted those units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the PJP were recruited from the regular police force. Younger men, physically fit for harder field missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that people were recruited from the regular police force. What were their regular lines of work before they joined the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beat policemen, patrolling, traffic police, duty service; the usual police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did these men have combat experience, or similar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say these men had been engaged in regular police work such as patrolling and going on the beat. Did they, therefore, need additional training to be able to take up their new jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course they needed training, because untrained people cannot be involved even in harder police work, let alone combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any training was conducted for these policemen who had come to assist in the situation that arose in your town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there was a later period when the staff set up a training centre for the PJP, and I believe it was on Mount Tara, a hotel called Sljivovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before this training centre on mount Tara, had there existed a training centre in that locality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was just a normal hotel until the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to go to that location, that hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Before 1992 I went to it when it was a normal hotel. And after that I didn't go. I didn't even have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we call up D415.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at the right-hand top corner. There is a code, DX. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means it's closed circulation. And DX means that it needs urgent action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What level of urgency in action does it indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: DX means that upon receiving the assignment contained in the dispatch not more than 12 hours should elapse before action is taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you now look at the lower portion of the document where we see different designations in block letters under number 2. What are these designations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the PJM staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This one is Pristina, Urosevac, Gnjilane. Just tell us, What do they designate? You don't have to enumerate all the towns.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These designations indicate SUPs, secretariats that are supposed to send men from the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a time when one of the highest ranking state officials came to your border crossing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the 16th of February, 1993, around -- sometime in the afternoon, then-prime minister of Serbia, Nikola Sainovic, came with his entourage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 2D1206, the first photograph from that exhibit. Your Honours, this is a set of individual photographs from Exhibit P1592.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us - we see four persons in this photograph - from the left to the right, can you identify these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the foreground is Mr. Sainovic. And the uniformed man behind him is the PJP commander, Branko Prljevic from SUP Uzice. Behind, in uniform, is the chief of public security department, Stojicic. And next to him is the minister of the interior, Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at the second photograph from this set.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Do you recognise anyone here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one close-up in uniform with the moustache is Mr. Vidoje Pantic from SUP Uzice. I don't know the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at photo number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in this photo, can you recognise the first person on the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the man behind my open hand?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Mr. Lukic, an employee of the public security department who was detached to Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In fact, could you repeat the name and where he worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mihajlo Lukic, employed with the public security department. And he was permanently located in Bajina Basta as a detached employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We have an interpretation problem, because the witness said twice which department this man worked in and we hear twice "public security."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies. It was the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is corrected, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I thank the interpreters, too. Could we now look at the photograph number 8 from this set.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us where this photo was taken? And these two men in uniform, can you identify them? Do you know which structures they worked for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a photo near the border crossing itself, near Djakovo, just before these events. In the blue uniform is a member of my station. And the one in the green uniform is a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at photo number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what we can see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is just above the bridge, and it was taken from the border-crossing Bajina Basta. Below these houses is the entrance point to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On this day we were discussing, the 16th of January, who was inside these houses? Was there any fire coming from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These houses were occupied by Bosniak forces just above the bridge. And you can see from the photograph they are firing. They were attacking, firing at people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like this set of photographs to be accepted, to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could you ask the witness to tell us exactly how and where he sees that firing takes place from these houses? Could you tell us where you see that anyone is firing from these houses, and from which house, and how you can see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just say one sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Depends on what it is, Mr. Petrovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it's a translation problem. The translation was not precise enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay, then we'll ask the -- let's check. Is it the line I refer to when the witness said what he saw on the photograph? Yes. Could we -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read to the witness what is -- how his words are translated. Is it about the houses occupied by the Bosniak forces, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I read to you how your answer was translated to us. "These houses were occupied by Bosniak forces just above the bridge. And you can see from the photograph they are firing. They were attacking, firing at people." Could you please correct what you consider to be wrong, because you're nodding "no." Could you please repeat your answer, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time of the attack there were Muslim forces inside these houses that opened fire on people crossing the bridge. That was at that time. And the photograph was taken later, much later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you can't see anything from this photograph as far as firing is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Because the photograph was not taken at the time of the shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic. The question, then, of course, arises what we can see on this photograph. I mean, the houses, what do they add to what the witness said already? But you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think I asked for this set of photographs to be admitted. And I would appreciate it if the Trial Chamber could rule. I think that was the last thing I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no objections from the Prosecution. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D1206 will receive number D744, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether even after the 16th January, 1993, there was shooting in the direction of the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know about the killing of this young man, Bogdanovic, below the Rasniste [phoen] settlement on the road. He was killed by a sniper bullet from the other side, from the Djurdjevac feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if there came a time when the Muslim forces were repelled and pushed back, away from Skelani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The action of VRS units and VJ units pushed them back, way back, after four or five days of these attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you just sit closer to the microphone so you are audible to the interpreters. Tell me, witness, did some units that were involved in these operations you just discussed use your border crossing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four or five days after these events we received notice, as was the common practice in extraordinary situations, and, indeed, in the evening a military convoy passed through from Bajina Basta, across Bajina Basta, towards Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said you received notice - from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the MUP of Serbia at the request of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which particular service of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the administration of border-crossing police. They were the only ones who could give us notice or issue orders to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Did you at any point find out what military unit this was, who was the commander of the unit, and whom they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of their crossing, we didn't know. But later on we heard it was commanded by, I think at the time he was a colonel, Colonel Mrksic, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What vehicles crossed via your border crossing as part of this military column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several trucks, four-wheel-drive vehicles. I think there were two Pragas and quite a lot of troops, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us whether in Bajina Basta there was a State Security Service of Serbia detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since my arrival in Bajina Basta in 1974, and I still think they -- they have a detachment there today, so throughout that period there was a state security detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And in 1993 do you know who was employed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Mr. Pero Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where were their offices, the offices of the state security detachment in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the premises of the Bajina Basta secretariat. So where all the other offices were, they had their offices as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You told us that on those premises the MUP staff was also established and located. In relation to their offices, can you tell us where the state security detachment was located within that building in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The staff itself was in an office that belonged to the chief of the secretariat because it was the biggest office. And then the following one was a set of offices used by the inspectors. And then was the detachment offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So they were all in the same hallway. The staff and the detachment were in the same hallway space?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you at any point get to meet Mr. Franko Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, not directly, really. But I know who he was, and I am familiar with his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In 1993 have you seen Mr. Simatovic in Bajina Basta? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him for the first time when Prime Minister Sainovic came to the border crossing. And then I've seen him on two or three occasions, maybe, in that very hallway when he would be visiting the staff commander. And I think once close to the hotel in the town centre. All together, three times maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, your answer is not fully transcribed. When did you see Mr. Simatovic in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him later, after I had seen him at the border crossing. It was maybe five or ten days after that, but I cannot be more precise about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion were you going anywhere or was maybe Simatovic going anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on my way to meet with the special unit's commander, and that's where I saw Mr. Simatovic in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you on any occasion find out -- have you found out on any occasion later why was Mr. Simatovic in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you see a man in -- on official premises, of course, one wants to know why is he there. And then later at the staff I was told that this was an employee of the state security department, and that was all I needed to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir: You told us that you saw Mr. Simatovic on several occasions; in which time-period all this happened? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be very precise. But between the arrival of the prime minister on the 16th of February and the end of May. So I've seen him two or three times altogether during that time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did at any point a group of international observers come to your border crossing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After the blockade of Republika Srpska was introduced - I think that must have been in mid-1993 - as of then, there were observers present there. And I think they remained there until mid-1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us, Where were they deployed, what was their role there, what did they do there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I knew, as far as I was advised by the Serbian MUP, their main task was to prevent passage of uniformed people or armed people either way. They were billeted in Drina hotel, and they worked at the very border crossing together with the customs officials. They were there 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who they reported to, the UN observers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot be precise, but I believe they were sending their reports to the United Nations. Whether the General Assembly or some other committee, I don't know. Security Council ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever received any reports about complaints made by the observers in relation to the activities of your men or events at the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never told about anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, have you heard about an airport in Skelani that may have been built in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What? An airport? I -- I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, 1993, or 1994, have you seen planes taking off or landing in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about transport of wounded people from Skelani to the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only way that the transport could have been made - and that's how it was made - was through the border crossing in vehicles. They would be taken to the health centre in Bajina Basta, and from there, in urgent cases, they would be transported by helicopters either to the military hospital in Belgrade or the clinical centre in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: These helicopters: Whose helicopters they were [as interpreted], and where would they take off from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was JA helicopters coming either from Ponikve or from Belgrade, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And from Bajina Basta where would they take off or land in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at a playground that was close to the health centre. That's also the place where the prime minister landed when he arrived in a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just take very brief instructions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Farr, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Almost, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seovac, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Farr. Mr. Farr is counsel for the Prosecution. I think I explained that already earlier to you. Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Seovac. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd like to start by asking you about your relationship with the DB, the State Security Service. When you were the commander of the Bajina Basta border police station, did you send written reports or other written communications to the State Security Service regarding any of your activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was duty-bound to submit reports only to my administrations. If it was occasionally necessary to report to them, then I would send such a report to the employee who was part of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And what kind of matters would that be about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly about incidents such as the attack, or threats to security coming from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And to whom precisely in the State Security Service would you send these reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the state security centre, Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was the chief of that centre at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that, for a while at least, a certain Sokic was in that position, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You said that you would send these reports "Mainly about incidents such as the attack, or threats to security coming from the other side." Other than attacks or threats from the other side, did you report to the State Security Service about any other matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trying to remember right now. It's very difficult to say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but if we look at the witness's answer on page 45, line 15, you will see that he said attacks and other issues. And I'm afraid that the interpretation given by my colleague is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly by interpretation -- the interpretation provided by the interpreters? Or ... Let me just see. Page 45, line 15 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague asked him whether he reported about anything else, not only the attacks. In his answer, the witness responded by saying that he reported about the attacks and he added something else. And I would like my colleague to put a clear question then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're saying Mr. Farr is misrepresenting the evidence. I just have to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that my colleague simplified what was in the transcript. I'm not saying that he misquoted anything. He just simplified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Farr, apparently there's an issue about you summarising too much the answer of the witness. Could you please put the question again to the witness and then include the whole of his previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I did. I'm comparing lines 15 and 16 to lines 23 and 24. But I'll put it again to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, the transcript - when I asked you what kind of matters that would be about, in other words, your reports - your answer was: "Mainly about incidents such as the attack, or threats to security coming from the other side." Other than those matters, what would you report to the state security about, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not in a position, I was not even authorised, since that was a different department, I was not in a position to make decisions as to I have to report about this or that. If I would be told by my chain of command to report, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And do you remember that ever happening with respect to anything other than "incidents such as the attack, or threats to security coming from the other side"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What kinds of things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, let me see, when the troops passed through, then attempts to prevent a larger group of entering or a group of people who were armed. If there were incidents like that, I would, upon receiving signals that I should, I would then report to the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You've discussed both Franko Simatovic and Obrad Stevanovic in your testimony. Were you ever personally present at a meeting at which both Mr. Stevanovic and Mr. Simatovic were also present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Were you ever at the Tara training camp any time in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you discussed the Muslim offensive or Army of B&H offensive in Skelani in January 1993 and the crimes committed by those forces in the course of that offensive. And I want to be clear with you that the Prosecution does not contest the existence of that offensive or the occurrence of the crimes or the suffering of the civilians who were victimised. I would now like to ask you briefly about your knowledge of some other events in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And could we please have P385 on the screen. This is operational directive number 4 of the Main Staff of the VRS, dated 19 November 1992. And if we could have page 7 in English -- well, let's look at the first page first. Okay. If we could now have page 7 in English, and e-court page 15, which is the second-to-last page in B/C/S. Your Honour, I see that this is almost illegible in B/C/S on our screens. I do have a hard copy that the witness can look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that there's no objection against giving a hard copy to the witness. Could the usher assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a question, though. If I'm not mistaken, how does anything in this document arise from my examination-in-chief? Maybe I spoke too soon, but I really don't see any such thing. Maybe my learned friend can help me with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, if you think the time is ripe to explain that to us, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is intended to contextualize the witness's evidence about the Muslim offensive on Skelani. It's also evidence in support of our case that I'm seeking to adduce pursuant to the second half of 90(H)(ii) -- 90(H)(i), apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, that -- Then you may proceed. Could the usher assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, if we can look first at the page that's been handed to you and if you direct your attention to the middle of the page, we'll see that this directive -- which is the bottom of the page in English, I should say -- this directive was drafted by Major-General Manojlo Milovanovic. And while it isn't physically signed, it appears to be from Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic, signing as commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could now have the bottom of page 5 in English and the top of e-court page 11 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, for you it's the page that has the yellow tape flag on it. I'll begin reading with item D. It says: "The Drina Corps, from its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad, the dam, Zvornik, and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population." Sir, were you aware that one of the tasks given by Ratko Mladic to the Drina Corps in November of 1992 was to force the Muslim population to leave this portion of Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I don't see a reason why I should know about that. All that was happening across the river in Republika Srpska, and I had absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to explain why you do not know something. If you don't know, you don't know. Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm that VRS operations in Eastern Bosnia in 1992 were in fact forcing the Muslim population out of certain portions of the territory, for example in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I have to say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You're not aware of the Muslim population being forced out of Skelani municipality in 1992 by the VRS; is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that because I joined the station on the 7th of October. You're talking about some events preceding my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You are aware, though, I take it, that the Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia was ultimately forced out by the VRS in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't confirm with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, could we -- Could I ask you the question a slightly different way. Were you aware that the Muslim population, by majority, left? So apart from what forced them out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the Muslim population was in the territory of Srebrenica and that those who were close to me were Serbs. I don't know how they had been separated from each other because I really wasn't there all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Skelani, was that a majority Muslim or Serb or Croat population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a mixed Muslim/Serb population. Before the war, the ratio was 35:65, or, rather, 55 in favour of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you talking about the village of Skelani or the area of Skelani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about Skelani as a municipality with the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the village of Skelani itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ratio was more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. And I've finished with that document, so we can get that back from the witness. Could we now -- and I'm moving on to another topic. Could we now please have on the screen 65 ter 6393.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, as you can see, this is a combat order for further operations from the command of the Drina Corps. It's dated 12 February 1993, so a little bit less than a month after the offensive that you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In the upper right-hand corner of the document, we see the Serbian word "Udar" in quotation marks. And I would also call the Chamber's attention to the number of this document, which is 01/5-97. That will be relevant to a document we'll look at shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, in your direct examination, at pages 39 and 40, you were asked about a counter-attack, and you indicated that there was a counter-attack and that to your knowledge the VRS and the VJ participated in that counter-attack. I'd like to read the first paragraph of this document. It says: "Number 1: Following the successful operations conducted by units of the corps, the enemy forces in the general area of Srebrenica, Skelani, Bratunac, Pobudje, Cerska, and Kamenica have sustained heavy losses, particularly in manpower. The enemy has also lost a large part of territory under its control prior to the offensive operations. Our forces control the area of Kamenica, most of the territory of Skelani municipality, Ilijin Brod, part of the area of Bratunac municipality in the direction of the villages of Kravica and Glogova, in the direction of the Sase Mine and the Caus feature. The enemy has lost its initiative and is now on the defensive." Sir, this is a description of the counter-attack that you described in your direct examination; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so. It was probably that. But I didn't know that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And the word "Udar" on the upper right-hand corner of this order is the name of the counter-attack operation; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I've never seen these documents. I'm not familiar with any of the activities described in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, during your direct examination you were asked: "... do you know if there came a time when the Muslim forces were repelled and pushed back, away from Skelani?" Your answer was: "The action of VRS units of and VJ units pushed them back, way back, after four or five days of these attacks." You were asked further questions about troops crossing your border, and you indicated that a group under the command of Colonel Mrksic crossed the border. Sir, isn't it correct that what you were describing was Operation Udar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was describing the crossing of the unit. I don't know anything about their further activities, nor was I in a position to know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this as a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We object to the exhibit. First of all, there's a huge amount of information in this exhibit which could mean many things. And we don't -- nobody knows but Mr. Farr what the Prosecution intend to use that document for other than this first paragraph, and even that, it's difficult to know what the Prosecution's intention is. If the Prosecution's intention is to use that paragraph to impeach the witness, it's difficult to know how that impeaches the witness. And if Mr. Farr intends to use that paragraph to prove something else, then, again, that hasn't been explained to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, when a document is admitted, the entire document is in evidence and all parties can rely on. The primary relevance of this document for us at this moment is the association of the name of the operation with the actions described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you need the rest of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there's a way to put it in evidence in a meaningful way without the rest of the document, then, no. I mean, that's what we're relying on it for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, it's a five-page document. Apparently you -- the first page will do, Mr. ... for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: There may be a signature on the document as well, but, I mean, anything that indicates what the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, tell us whether there is. I would say that there seems to be a signature on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So perhaps the signature -- the signature block and the stamp. But not the remaining paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So pages 1 and 5 is what you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, does your objection stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If the point is to demonstrate or to suggest that the witness was talking about Operation Udar and the first paragraph and the signature enables that submission to be made, then we don't object.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be clear: This is not being tendered solely for impeachment; this is being tendered as substantive evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But then we do object to that because for what purpose? Who knows? Nobody knows but Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I think it will become clear shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then what we'll do is the following: We'll reserve a number for those portions of this document that will finally survive, and we'll first listen to the other questions Mr. Farr will put to the witness. And the number would be, Madam Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for the portions of document 6393 will receive number P3085.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll later know whether it's the whole of the document or whether it's just the pages 1 and 5, in which case, of course, it would have to be re-uploaded. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm moving on to another document now to contextualize this one. I don't know -- this document has been marked as P3085; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that's the best way of doing it. And then we'll later find out whether it's the whole of the document or part of it which will be admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, the number just you reserved is the number to be assigned for this document which is now marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we now please have P392 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, to orient you, we're looking --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sorry, if we could have page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, to orient you: We're about to look at an excerpt from a notebook kept by the Ratko Mladic, and the particular entry we're looking at is dated 28 February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The portion I'm interested in is at the bottom of the page in both languages. So if we could zoom in as much as possible on the bottom half.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I, sir, do have a hard copy of this document as well if you would prefer that. I don't know whether you're able to read this or not. This entry is from Sunday, the 28th of February, 1993. It gives the location as Tara. And the caption of the entry is: "Plan of action in Operation Udar." Mladic lists those present as: "Panic, myself, Ojdanic, Loncar," whose name is unfortunately misspelled in the English translation, "Tkac, Frenki, and two men from the MUP." Sir, do we agree that Zivota Panic was the chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and Ratko Mladic was the chief of the Main Staff of the VRS at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose so. I don't know. I was not an army member, so I don't know anything about any of the two militaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Are you able to comment in any way on the question of whether Badza and Obrad Stevanovic are the two men from the MUP who are listed in this entry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'll now just read briefly from the entry. The first two lines say: "The units are in certain sectors and garrisons." "In Osmace, Jadar, and Kragivode use PO, and in Kragivode use napalm." Sir, Kragivode is a village in Skelani municipality; correct?
