utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it belongs to Skelani or perhaps Srebrenica, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: But in any event, it's a village in the vicinity of the border where you worked; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It would be about 30 kilometres away from where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, I think we may have gone past the point of a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you're right. We take a break, and we resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, could you give the Chamber any impression about how long you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a topic that I would like to address that was not covered during the witness's direct examination. I would estimate two hours from now, if the Chamber would grant me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems to me it was the practice with viva voce witnesses the time allowed for examination-in-chief is the same as the time allowed for cross-examination. Maybe I'm mistaken, but I believe that was the case during the Prosecution case. I've spent one hour in my examination-in-chief, and I believe that is something that should be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Petrovic, I didn't say that the two hours were allowed. I said "you may proceed" after a moment of silent thinking, you may have noticed that. I further discussed the matter with my colleagues. And, of course, much depends on what Mr. Farr is -- is -- what the matter is he would like to -- he would like to put to the witness. I, by the way, saw that Mr. Jordash was on his feet as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I was going to support Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Farr, any further explanation as to why you use quite some time in cross-examination, where the examination-in-chief was limited in time? And to some extent even dealt with matters which, although we found out that only later, are not even in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that this witness can give us important and relevant testimony. Not all of it arises from the direct examination. Obviously it's for the Chamber to decide whether it's a good use of Court time or not, but I -- we would submit that the length of direct examination should not be a per se rule as to how much time is granted in cross. I would also note that we've generally been coming in under our estimates. This is an extraordinary application; we recognise that. And we don't ask for this kind of thing often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we will further look also at our database with all the details of the -- the details of the time used. Apart from that, Mr. Petrovic, of course, your initial time scheduled was two hours. That's -- to some extent, of course, the other party orients itself on the time which was announced by the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I agree. But I believe what matters are the topics opened up in examination-in-chief. It is true we announced originally two hours, but it's also true that we're trying to follow the instructions to focus and use time as efficiently as possible. I believe the topics are really the basis for -- for estimates, not time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I do not know them yet. And I do not know whether you know them already, but Mr. Farr said that he would elicit evidence on matters I'm not aware of yet. Let's -- let's see -- Mr. Farr, there is a clear flag here. And then, again, I say not that you get your two hours, but you've at least the next 45 minutes to demonstrate how efficient and how focussed you are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, just to reorient you: We were discussing the meeting at Tara on the 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could now have the next page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I'll now continue reading with the portion that begins with the initials ZP, which we say indicates that the speaker is Zivota Panic. It says: "ZP: We cannot go into action until we are 100 percent certain with minimal losses. "Everyone must in position by Thursday. "The men from the MUP shall be a part of TG-1 Mrksic. "Everything should be ready for action by Thursday." Sir, are you able to say whether this is the Colonel Mrksic you described crossing the Drina River with troops and vehicles as part of the counter-attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot claim that, because I have no idea about this meeting, who participated, and what was discussed. I had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Turning to your evidence about Mr. Simatovic's presence in Bajina Basta. During the time that he was there, did you ever hear anyone claiming or alleging that he financed or controlled some kind of special unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You said you saw him on a few occasions. How was he dressed when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I saw him, when he was accompanying the prime minister, he was in uniform. And the other two or three times that I saw him he was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that on that first occasion he was dressed like a combatant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in uniform. I don't remember if he had any equipment, but if -- I don't know. It was -- it was the uniform for field purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And on that occasion you mentioned the presence, I think, of Sainovic. You may have mentioned Sokolovic as well. Jovica Stanisic was also present; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to read you something that you are recorded as saying on the video of that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm reading now from the transcript of P1592.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, you're describing the attack and the fleeing civilians, and you say the following: "We were practically eye-witnesses of this attack against the civilians, against those women and children. Whenever we had the chance, we jumped out of the trenches to rescue those ..." And then Sainovic says: "... those people." You continue: "Yes. Yes. We carried them up to here. I did not have the possibility to evacuate them by car because we had just one car at our disposal. But there were vehicles from our rear area." Sir, based on that, it sounds likes you risked physical injury or possibly even death to assist those people. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, as a policeman it was my duty to assist people whose life was in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And as the commander of the border police station, you allowed those people to remain in Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not that I allowed them. They came in en masse. And a few days later, when that area was liberated for them, they returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: When they came in, did you check them for papers to see whether they had any legal right to be in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If somebody is shooting at you and at them, would you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I take that as a no, sir; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this document is a cable from Vukoja Vukovic who is identified as the commander of Tactical Group 1. The document is addressed to the Drina Corps commander and it's dated 6 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could have the middle of page two in B/C/S and the top of page 2 in English. And I'm interested in item 5 specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, I'll just read you paragraph 5 of this cable. It says: "Allegedly, some intervention unit exists in Skelani (in the camp). There are 57 troops from the Skelani municipality wearing the so-called red berets and commanded by Frenki and Bozovic. They are all military conscripts of the Skelani battalion, but they have not spent a day in it. I request of the addressee to sort this issue out urgently with the Main Staff. If I could get those 57 troops to my battalion, it would get invigorated, and many problems from which this unit had suffered from the begin would get sorted out." Sir, in May of 1993, Franko Simatovic and Rajo Bozovic commanded a unit that was commonly known as the Red Berets based at the school in Skelani and that unit included a number of men who were supposed to have been serving with the VRS Skelani Independent Battalion; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm completely unaware of this. Those were units of the Army of Republika Srpska, and I couldn't possibly know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that you never heard anything about it, of these claims being made by the commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge whatsoever about what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we now please have P399 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this document is a report dated 15 May 1993. So that's nine days after the previous document. Whereas the last document was from Tactical Group 1, this document indicates that it is from the Independent Skelani Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And can we have please have page 3 in B/C/S and page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Whereas the last document was from Vukoja Vukovic, the commander of Tactical group 1, if we scroll down to the bottom of these pages we can see that this document is from Lieutenant-Colonel Branko Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we scroll to the right in B/C/S, we'll see his name. And now could we please return to the top of the first page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, were you at least aware of the existence of the Independent Skelani Battalion of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the unit was called, but I knew there was a unit of battalion strength. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And how far was their headquarters from your border-crossing post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where specifically their headquarters was. Do you have a location?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, I don't. I'm asking you. But you've said you don't know, so I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The title of this report is: "Report on the Establishment of the Units for Special Purposes, Red Berets of the MUP of Serbia in Skelani." And I'll start reading at the beginning of the report: "The Red Berets unit was established on 8 June 1992. It had 20 military conscripts and was under the command of three instructors who trained its soldiers. The unit continued to grow and there are 50 soldiers in the camp in the school now." Sir, how far was the school in Skelani from your border post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About two kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Skipping down a few lines, it says: "15 soldiers from the camp secure the KIK facility while the rest are in the camp. During the attack on Jezero, two soldiers were killed at KIK and one was killed in the attack on Skelani on 16 January 1993. After the unit left the Jezero facility, they left this area and went to Tara for further training. "The unit returned to Skelani in February and was again stationed in the school. The unit was under the command of Bozovic. It had 150 soldiers and 52 of them were from Skelani (their names are in the attachment)." Sir, here we have a lieutenant-colonel in the VRS reporting to the Drina Corps command about a unit called the Red Berets which he says was stationed in a school that you say was two kilometres from your workplace. And you really never heard any of this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Never heard of the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could now have the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'll begin reading with the sentence, "They took part in combat operations." It says: "They took part in combat operations at," and then as it's written here, "Kraglivode. Afterwards, they took part in the mopping up of the train around Radenovice when two soldiers from the unit originally from Novi Sad were killed." Sir, in the notebook entry, the Mladic notebook entry we looked at a few minutes ago, we saw a reference to Kragivode in the context of Operation Udar. Here we see a reference to this unit participating in combat in Kraglivode. Sir, the truth is, Mr. Simatovic didn't just participate in the planning of the counter-attack you described. The unit that he and Bozovic commanded actually took part in that fighting in co-ordination with the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object. My learned friend is asking the witness to make conclusions and analyse evidence. I don't see how he would be able to do that. Also, the witness has said several times exactly what he knows about it and yet my colleague continues asking the same questions again. And, ultimately, the witness is being asked to analyse the evidence in this case which, I believe, is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think, as a matter of fact, that the witness is asked to do that. Let me just re-read ... He presents something to the witness and then puts a very leading question to the question, which he is entitled to do in cross-examination. Mr. Farr, you may proceed. Or you can -- I think the witness has not yet answered the question. Or did he?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: He has not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Farr suggested to you in his question that the unit that he said Mr. Stanisic [sic] and Mr. Bozovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Bozovic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- I apologise. -- that that unit actually took part in the fighting in co-ordination with the VRS and that was a unit in which Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Bozovic were involved. Is that -- can you confirm that? It's suggested to you by Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm this. And I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, I'll just read you one more sentence from this document. This is the sentence that's at the top of the page in English, and it begins with the words "In addition to apprehending persons ..." That sentence reads: "In addition to apprehending persons who refuse to go into combat, they also control the bridge." Sir, it's our position that given the location of your border police station, you must have known about this unit, and you're claiming not to in order to assist the accused. Would you like to comment or respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me, please. In the original document, we read: "The RS MUP." In the translation, we read: "The MUP of the Republic of Serbia." "RS MUP" can stand both for the MUP of the Republic of Serbia as well as the MUP of the Republika Srpska, and I believe that this is something that the witness should be aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Perhaps he could first respond to the proposition that I put to him, and then I'll move on to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then move further.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So, going back to my question, sir. It was based on the sentence of this document that says: "In addition to apprehending persons who refuse to go into combat, they also control the bridge." And then I told you that it's our position that given where you worked, you must have known about the existence of this unit, and you're claiming not to in order to assist the accused. And if you'd like to comment on or respond to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific and tell me which side of the bridge did that unit control? When it says "control" here, what side of the bridge is referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Well, sir, we only know what the document says. But our position would be that even if this was a unit on the other side of the bridge, you would probably have known about their existence. Even if you were at one end of the bridge and they were at the other end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On our side, my police station and my unit had the exclusive right to control the bridge and the traffic. On the other side of the bridge, which was a war-struck area, control was carried out by ad hoc units that found themselves there. There was no permanent police station as we had, which means today there was one unit, the following day there was somebody else. On our side, in our police station, we never knew who would be there. In principle, it was the military police of the Army of the Republika Srpska. And -- and the Republika Srpska MUP as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: All right. And just one more quote from this report. This portion reads: "They returned to camp on 14 May 1993, but refused to put themselves at the command of the SBS," which the interpreter has indicated is Skelani Independent Battalion, "saying that only the MUP RS" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a sound coming from somewhere of which I do not know what it is, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be the witness with the case for his glasses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can't see that from here. We constantly hear your -- your ... what seems to be the box of your glasses. It has been resolved. Thank you very much, witness. Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll just repeat the quote from the beginning. The quote that we're interested in says: "They returned to camp on 14 May 1993, but refused to put themselves at the command of the SBS ... saying that only the MUP RS can be their commander because this is what they had supposedly been told when they set out to return to Skelani." Sir, are you able to commend on that excerpt in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were reports sent by military units, and I'm in no position to provide any comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this may be overly cautious, but I've reached a point in my examination where it may be appropriate to advise the witness pursuant to Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all extra mikes be switched off. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Farr says that he's going to put some questions to you where he does not exclude for the possibility that you might wish to object against making a statement because it might tend to incriminate yourself. Now, if a question is put to you and if a truthful answer would be incriminating for yourself, then you may object to answer that question. And the Chamber will then consider your objection and act in accordance with the Rules. I'm not yet telling you exactly what that is, because that could go in various directions, but please be aware that if you are -- if your answer would incriminate yourself, that is, that you would expose yourself to further investigation or even prosecution, that you may object to answer that question. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Petrovic, yes, is there -- is it a matter you could raise with the witness having his earphones on?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that -- [In English] Your Honour, I believe that that's not the problem, because I would just like to suggest to have this portion of his testimony in private session just because of reasons witness gave as possible reasons for protective measures, if that's in Chamber's favour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I invited the witness at the beginning when we were dealing with protective measures to state any -- any reasons that he thought we might need to have those protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: He didn't raise these matters as a reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that you may not have understood exactly what Mr. Petrovic was hinting at. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I hereby now publicly announce that we adjourn. And we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 22nd of February, 9.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom, II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of February, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
